initial_presentation: A 63-year-old male with a 20-year history of diabetes mellitus and ischemic heart disease was admitted after experiencing several health issues. He had been in good health and completed a Hajj pilgrimage, but a few months after returning, he began to suffer from abdominal colic, which was initially suspected to be cholecystitis but remained unconfirmed. The patient reported a poor appetite, abdominal pain, loose stools, a weight loss of approximately 7 kg over one year, fatigue, and headaches. He later developed slowness of gait, falls, subjective weakness on the left side of his body, balance issues, slurred speech, involuntary movements of the eyes, face, and limbs, and difficulty swallowing, characterized by coughing while swallowing. He also exhibited a lack of initiative, forgetfulness for recent events, and visual hallucinations that were non-stereotyped and recurrent. He was treated for Parkinson's disease at a regional hospital without improvement. As his condition worsened, he was brought to our center. Upon admission, his HMSE score was 19. Clinical examination revealed involuntary, disconjugate, arrhythmic eye movements, eyebrow lifting, dyskinetic movements of the upper lips and cheeks, mild shoulder elevation, and occasional trunk twisting. He had skew deviation of the eyes, saccadic initiation defects, broken saccades, slow vertical saccades, and multiple saccadic oscillations. He exhibited a tendency to stoop forward, swayed while walking with two-person support, had anteroposterior trunk movements while sitting, mild finger-nose incoordination, and completely illegible, effortless speech diagnosed as mixed dysarthria with intermittent drooling and choking. He had poor respiratory support while speaking, poor lip seal, and slow tongue movements. General examination revealed itchy, scaly skin lesions with nodularity, pigmentation, and serous ooze over the scalp, cheek, nose, and chin, which were slightly tender.

A 20-month-old girl was referred to our center with symptoms of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS). She exhibited eyelid swelling and abdominal distension. Corticosteroid therapy had been initiated for nephrotic syndrome at a local hospital. Upon admission, physical examination revealed a low nasal bridge, broad nasal tip, very short stature with a short trunk, hyperpigmented skin macules, and corneal opacities.

A 16-year-old male with no prior health issues presented with severe pain, stiffness, and muscle twitching in both lower extremities for over a month. The pain, which was burning and non-radiating, began gradually and became continuous within days. It increased with walking short distances and was not alleviated by rest or prescribed pain medications. The stiffness was more pronounced below the knees than in the thighs. He also experienced pain on touch and sensitivity to cold, which worsened his discomfort, described as a wavy sensation in the extremities. The patient reported episodic twitching throughout the body, particularly in the calves, chest, and around the mouth, which intensified with movement. There were no issues with urinary or fecal incontinence, seizures, speech, or vision. His medical, surgical, and family history were unremarkable. Sleep was disrupted due to calf pain and nocturia. On admission, he was restless and in significant discomfort but alert and oriented. Vital signs included a pulse of 114 BPM, BP of 155/100 mmHg, and a respiratory rate of 20/minute. Muscle strength was normal in the upper extremities and lower extremities above the knee but slightly reduced below the knee bilaterally. Reflexes were active in the brachioradialis, biceps, triceps, and ankle but diminished at the knee. Plantar reflexes were absent bilaterally. Muscle bulk was symmetrical, and tone was normal. He reported decreased pin-prick sensation in the toes and fingers of both lower extremities, but joint position sense was intact. Coordination and cranial nerves two through twelve were normal, with no nystagmus or tremors observed. The patient had an antalgic gait. Physical examination revealed desquamating, blanchable erythema on both feet. There were no signs of jaundice, edema, organ enlargement, or lymph node enlargement. Abdominal, respiratory, and cardiovascular examinations were normal.

A 51-year-old female patient, who has had three pregnancies and two live births, came to the clinic with complaints of vaginal itching, irritation, and a tearing sensation near the top of the vaginal area, persisting for one year. She noted that the discomfort varied in intensity over time but had become more severe in recent months. She did not report any excessive vaginal odor, general pelvic pain, fever, or chills, and had no concerns about sexually transmitted infections. The patient mentioned that physical activity and moisture from daily swimming exacerbated her discomfort. Upon physical examination, a 1.5 cm firm bilateral vulvar lesion with shallow red ulcerations was observed at the lower mons pubis.

The patient is a 3-year-old boy of Pakistani descent, born at term following an uneventful pregnancy. His parents reported no consanguinity. During a routine analysis conducted for language delay and concerns related to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), the patient exhibited very low serum uric acid levels (<0.2 mg/dL), which were subsequently confirmed.

A 24-year-old woman visited the Reproductive Endocrinology Department due to a gradually enlarging right ovarian cyst, measuring 3 cm in diameter. This cyst and a uterine developmental abnormality were identified a year earlier at a local hospital. Despite these findings, she wished to pursue pregnancy, as her tumor biomarker levels were normal and she had not undergone further examinations or treatments. She began menstruating at age 13 and experienced regular menstrual cycles every 30 days, lasting 7 days, with mild dysmenorrhea that sometimes required medication. A gynecological examination revealed a normal vulva, vagina, and cervix. The uterus was of normal size, with the right corpus slightly larger than the left.

A 41-year-old woman presented to the ER with a 4-week history of dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. She had a past medical history of antiphospholipid syndrome associated with spontaneous abortions but was otherwise in good health.

A 2-month-old male presented with a 3-day history of cough, 2 days of rapid breathing and poor feeding, and 1 day of fever. He had intermittent fever starting from day 4 of life, accompanied by a dry, non-paroxysmal cough. The antenatal and birth history were normal, with a birth weight of 3000 g, and he was discharged on day 2 of life. During the first week, he exhibited a weak cry and reduced spontaneous movement in all four limbs. Developmentally, he did not achieve neck holding but showed regard for his mother's face, responded to sound, and followed objects. The family history revealed that he was the third child in a non-consanguineous marriage, with two male siblings who had early infantile deaths at 50 and 90 days, respectively, following a history of hypotonia. On examination, he had a heart rate of 143/min, respiratory rate of 68/min, and oxygen saturation of 50% on room air. His weight was 3.6 kg (-3 Z score), length 58 cm (0.88 Z score), and occipitofrontal circumference 36.2 cm (-2.5 Z score). Muscle weakness was noted with a frog-like posture, jug-handle deformity of the upper limbs, bilateral wrist contracture, bell-shaped chest, and poor spontaneous activity. He was awake and alert with spontaneous eye-opening, extra-ocular movements, and no ptosis or facial weakness. Tongue fasciculations and flabby skeletal muscles were present. Hypotonia was indicated by head lag when pulled to sit, dangling legs on ventral suspension, and head lying below the plane of the body on horizontal suspension. There were minimal spontaneous distal movements and no antigravity movements. Deep tendon reflexes were absent, and bilateral plantar responses were mute. Sensations were intact, and there was no nystagmus. Respiratory examination showed nasal flaring, bell-shaped chest, bilateral suprasternal, intercostal, and subcostal retractions with a seesaw breathing pattern, indicating intercostal muscle weakness. Chest auscultation revealed decreased air entry with bilateral crackles.

A 42-year-old woman presented with firm, brown-colored tumorous nodules on her bilateral lower extremities. The patient started noticing the growths after sustaining some insect bites in these areas. The dermatologist she initially visited treated her with triamcinolone injection and steroid tape. However, the patient did not respond to treatment, and the nodules did not soften or reduce in size. When she later visited our outpatient department in Nippon Medical School Hospital, the examination revealed dark brown-colored nodular lesions on bilateral knees, the right tibial region, dorsum of the left foot, the right calcaneal area, and the lateral side of the left foot. The nodules on her lower extremities manifested in one of two ways; the first type of nodule appeared very similar to keloids, but the other type was partially rounded in shape, unlike a usual keloid.
A 25-year-old female patient presented with a 2-month history of gradual, painless, progressive reduction in vision along with floaters in the left eye.
